title: The War of the Worlds
author: H. G. Wells
setting: Surrey and London across about three weeks, from a sandpit on Horsell Common to the top of Primrose Hill
lengthNote: Two books and twenty-seven chapters, the last of them an epilogue written years after the events
openingLine: No one would have believed in the last years of the nineteenth century that this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences greater than man’s and yet as mortal as his own; that as men busied themselves about their various concerns they were scrutinised and studied, perhaps almost as narrowly as a man with a microscope might scrutinise the transient creatures that swarm and multiply in a drop of water.
summary: A cylinder from Mars lands on a Surrey common, and within a week the largest empire on Earth has been reduced to six million people running along the roads out of London. Wells tells it through a narrator who is never in charge of anything: he watches, runs, hides in a ruined scullery and arrives too late to understand what he has seen. The Martians are killed by bacteria, and the book is careful to insist that this is not a victory.
referenceStyle: book and chapter, e.g. Book I, Chapter XVII

sourceText.label: Standard Ebooks text of The War of the Worlds
sourceText.note: The novel divides into Book I, The Coming of the Martians, and Book II, The Earth Under the Martians. Chapters are numbered in Roman within each book and carry titles, which references here give where they help.

atAGlance.label: Serialised
atAGlance.note: In Pearson's Magazine in Britain and Cosmopolitan in the United States, before any book edition.

atAGlance.label: First book edition
atAGlance.note: Published in London by William Heinemann.

atAGlance.label: Where it starts
atAGlance.note: Ordinary common land on the edge of the Surrey town where Wells was living when he planned the book.

atAGlance.label: How it ends
atAGlance.note: No army defeats the Martians. They die of the microbes every human body has already survived.

structure.label: Book I, Chapters I-IV
structure.title: A light on Mars, and a cylinder in a sandpit
structure.summary: Ten flashes are seen on Mars and reported as a curiosity. The first cylinder lands at night on Horsell Common, a crowd gathers round the pit as it would round a beached whale, and the lid begins to unscrew while the narrator watches from the heather.

scenes.title: The Eve of the War
scenes.summary: The narrator, writing afterwards, describes a world being studied by minds it has never thought about.

scenes.title: The Falling Star
scenes.summary: The cylinder comes down in the small hours and Ogilvy is the first man to reach it.

scenes.title: On Horsell Common
scenes.summary: A holiday crowd assembles round the pit and the newspapers get a paragraph.

scenes.title: The Cylinder Opens
scenes.summary: The first Martian hauls itself out and the watchers discover what they have come to see.

structure.label: Book I, Chapters V-VIII
structure.title: The Heat-Ray, and the evening papers
structure.summary: A deputation walks towards the pit under a white flag and is burned where it stands. The narrator gets home, tells his wife, and finds that the rest of England is still treating the matter as local news; the second cylinder falls while Woking is being evacuated.

scenes.title: The Heat-Ray
scenes.summary: An invisible beam kills the deputation and sets the common alight.

scenes.title: The Heat-Ray in the Chobham Road
scenes.summary: The crowd on the road is caught in the open.

scenes.title: How I Reached Home
scenes.summary: The narrator walks back through burning heather and finds his own dining room unchanged.

scenes.title: Friday Night
scenes.summary: London reads a short paragraph and goes to bed.

structure.label: Book I, Chapters IX-XIV
structure.title: The fighting-machines, and the brother’s story begins
structure.summary: The fighting-machines rise and the military answer is over almost before it begins. The narrator drives his wife to Leatherhead, comes back into the storm, meets the curate among the ruins of Weybridge, and the narrative opens a second front with his brother in London.

scenes.title: The Fighting Begins
scenes.summary: Guns are dug in on the common; the narrator takes his wife out of Woking.

scenes.title: In the Storm
scenes.summary: A tripod overtakes the dog cart in the lightning.

scenes.title: At the Window
scenes.summary: Soldiers pass the house and the artilleryman tells what happened to his battery.

scenes.title: What I Saw of the Destruction of Weybridge and Shepperton
scenes.summary: A Martian is brought down by artillery, and the river boils.

scenes.title: How I Fell in with the Curate
scenes.summary: A clergyman reads the invasion as the day of judgement and cannot stop talking.

scenes.title: In London
scenes.summary: The narrator's brother finds the capital calm, then reads the morning papers.

structure.label: Book I, Chapters XV-XVII
structure.title: Six million people on the roads
structure.summary: The Black Smoke clears the ground in front of the machines and London empties north and east. With the brother’s chapters the novel widens from one man’s escape to a study of a population in motion, and the Thunder Child gives the book its single moment of successful resistance.

scenes.title: What Had Happened in Surrey
scenes.summary: The Black Smoke is used systematically to kill anything that stays indoors.

scenes.title: The Exodus from London
scenes.summary: The brother joins the stampede and gets two women out through Barnet to the coast.

scenes.title: The Thunder Child
scenes.summary: A torpedo ram rams a fighting-machine and covers the escaping steamers.

structure.label: Book II, Chapters I-V
structure.title: Trapped with the curate
structure.summary: A fifth cylinder buries the narrator and the curate in a half-collapsed house at Sheen, with a Martian pit on the other side of the wall. For a fortnight the two men watch the invaders feed, ration a dwindling larder and quarrel, until the curate's noise forces the narrator to stop him.

scenes.title: Under Foot
scenes.summary: The narrator is hunted through Sheen and takes shelter in an empty house.

scenes.title: What We Saw from the Ruined House
scenes.summary: Through a crack in the wall the Martians are seen taking human blood.

scenes.title: The Days of Imprisonment
scenes.summary: Hunger, thirst and the curate's voice become the immediate danger.

scenes.title: The Death of the Curate
scenes.summary: The narrator strikes him with the handle of a chopper, and a Martian takes the body.

scenes.title: The Stillness
scenes.summary: The pit is abandoned and the narrator crawls out into a red landscape.

structure.label: Book II, Chapters VI-VII
structure.title: The red weed, and the artilleryman
structure.summary: Walking through the red weed, the narrator works out that he is no longer a master but an animal among animals. On Putney Hill he meets the artilleryman again, listens for a night to a magnificent scheme for living underground and rebuilding the species, then looks at the trench the man has actually dug.

scenes.title: The Work of Fifteen Days
scenes.summary: The red weed has taken the Thames valley and the narrator understands what has happened to his species.

scenes.title: The Man on Putney Hill
scenes.summary: The artilleryman's underground future, his champagne, and his unfinished tunnel.

structure.label: Book II, Chapters VIII-X
structure.title: Dead London, and the epilogue
structure.summary: The narrator walks into an empty capital following a howling that stops mid-note, climbs Primrose Hill and finds the Martians dead in their redoubt. The last chapter is written years later by a man who cannot walk down a road without seeing it silent.

scenes.title: Dead London
scenes.summary: The cry of Ulla, ulla ends, and the invaders are found killed by bacteria.

scenes.title: Wreckage
scenes.summary: The narrator breaks down, is taken in at Leatherhead, and gets home to Woking.

scenes.title: The Epilogue
scenes.summary: Unfinished science, a warning about the next opposition, and a man who wakes cold in the night.

characters.name: The narrator
characters.role: A writer on philosophical subjects, living near Woking
characters.summary: A man whose profession is explaining things and who spends the whole invasion failing to. He is never given a name, never holds a weapon that works and never makes a decision that alters events; what he does instead is look carefully and write it down years afterwards, which is the only kind of authority the book allows anyone.
characters.clue: He explains the Zodiac to his wife on a warm evening, and later beats a clergyman senseless in a scullery to stop him being heard.

characters.name: The narrator's brother
characters.summary: He exists so that the book can leave Surrey. His chapters are the only place where the invasion is seen as a problem of crowds, trains, money and roads, not of one frightened man, and he is also the only character who does something plainly useful: he gets two women out alive.
characters.clue: A London medical student who knocks a man down over a dropped bag of sovereigns and then drives two strangers to the coast.
traits: the book's second pair of eyes

characters.name: Ogilvy
characters.summary: He sees the first jet of gas leave Mars and tells the narrator that the chances against anything manlike there are a million to one. He is the first man to reach the cylinder and one of the first killed by the Heat-Ray, which is the book's briskest way of dealing with confident expertise.
characters.clue: He invites a friend up to look through a telescope, scoffs at the idea of signals from Mars, and dies under a white flag.

characters.name: The curate
characters.role: A clergyman met in the ruins of Weybridge
characters.summary: He meets the invasion with a theology that cannot hold it and collapses into repetition, appetite and noise. Wells does not let the narrator feel superior for long: the two men eat the same rations, and the killing in the scullery is done for the very practical reason that the curate can be heard.
characters.clue: He rebuilt his church three years ago, cannot stop asking why, and eats more than his share in the dark.

characters.name: The artilleryman
characters.role: A survivor of a gun battery destroyed on the common
characters.summary: Twice met and twice differently judged. On the second meeting he lays out a whole underground civilisation of able men who will learn to fly a fighting-machine, and the narrator is carried away by it until morning, when the plan turns out to consist of a short tunnel, a stolen larder and a game of cards.
characters.clue: He can describe the coming underground republic in detail, and has dug about ten yards of it.

characters.name: The Martians
characters.summary: Heads and hands with no digestive system, moving in machines because Earth's gravity is too heavy for their bodies. They are never given speech, motive or negotiation; the book insists they are neither devils nor monsters but a species whose planet is dying and which is doing what our own has done to other populations.
characters.clue: They cannot walk upright on this planet, take their nourishment straight from other creatures' veins, and are killed by something too small to see.

characters.name: The narrator's wife
characters.role: Left at Leatherhead in the second week
characters.summary: She is driven to relatives for safety in the third chapter of the invasion and is off the page for most of the book, which is exactly what makes the last line work. The narrator counts her among the dead, and she counts him among the dead, for longer than either of them is actually missing.
characters.clue: She has the signal lights of the railway pointed out to her on a warm evening, and is left with cousins at Leatherhead.

themes.name: Imperial reversal
themes.summary: Wells puts readers at the centre of the largest empire on Earth in the other position. Wells makes the argument explicit in the first chapter, naming the extermination of the Tasmanians before a single cylinder has landed, so that everything the Martians do afterwards has already been described as something Europeans did first.
themes.development: Stated as history in Book I, Chapter I; enacted as roads, refugees and confiscated homes in the exodus chapters; and left unresolved at the end, because the deliverance is bacterial, not moral.

themes.name: Dethronement
themes.summary: The invasion’s real damage is to a belief, more than a city: the belief that human beings are the point of the planet. The narrator dates his own loss of it precisely, standing among the red weed and realising that he has become an animal among animals, and the epilogue shows the feeling has not lifted.
themes.development: Complacency in Chapter I, terror in the middle books, and then a settled and permanent change of position in Book II, Chapters VI and X.

themes.name: Technological asymmetry
themes.summary: Courage makes no difference to the outcome of any engagement in this novel. The Heat-Ray kills before it is understood, the Black Smoke is applied like a weedkiller, and the one human success, the Thunder Child, is achieved by a ship that simply runs at a machine and dies doing it.
themes.development: Artillery at Horsell, a lucky shot at Shepperton, an ironclad off the Essex coast: three attempts, each smaller in its effect than the scale of the force behind it.

themes.name: Witness and report
themes.summary: Everything in the book reaches the reader through somebody who was there and did not understand it at the time. Telegraph, newspaper, rumour and eyewitness are all shown failing in different ways, and the narrator's authority comes from admitting how much of his account is reconstruction.
themes.development: A paragraph in the Daily Telegraph, then contradictory special editions, then no papers at all; and behind them the brother's narrative, which the narrator can only have received second-hand.

themes.name: Evolution and the humblest things
themes.summary: The novel's science is Darwinian before it is mechanical. Mars is old and cooling, its inhabitants have specialised themselves into brains with hands, and Earth's advantage turns out to be an immune system bought by a billion deaths nobody remembers.
themes.development: The cooling planet in Chapter I, the red weed rotting in Book II, and the Martians dead in the redoubt without a shot fired at them.

themes.name: Faith, explanation and nerve
themes.summary: Three ways of meeting a catastrophe are set against each other: the curate's apocalypse, the artilleryman's grand programme and the narrator's habit of writing down what he can see. Two of them are exposed, and the third is not offered as heroism, only as the one that leaves a record.
themes.development: The curate breaks in Book I, Chapter XIII and is silenced in Book II, Chapter IV; the artilleryman is believed for one night and disbelieved by breakfast.

techniques.name: Retrospective first-person narration
techniques.definition: A narrator telling, years later, events he lived through without understanding them.
techniques.inThisBook: The opening sentence is written from a future the first readers had not reached, which lets Wells put dread and explanation in the same paragraph without either cancelling the other.

techniques.name: Second narrator
techniques.definition: Breaking off one character's account to follow another who can see what the first cannot.
techniques.inThisBook: The brother’s three chapters take the reader to London and the coast, and they are the only way the novel can show six million people on the move.

techniques.name: Real places
techniques.definition: Using real, checkable place names, not invented ones.
techniques.inThisBook: Horsell, Ottershaw, Byfleet, Shepperton, Barnet, Putney Hill and Primrose Hill let a first reader trace the invasion across a map they already owned.

techniques.name: Shift of scale
techniques.definition: Moving between the astronomical and the domestic inside a few sentences.
techniques.inThisBook: Forty million miles of void in one paragraph and a siphon of soda water on a table in the next; later, a balloonist's view of London and then one man's thirst.

techniques.name: Domestic similes
techniques.definition: Describing something unprecedented by comparing it with a familiar household object.
techniques.inThisBook: The first fighting-machine is a milking stool bowled violently along the ground, and the spreading Black Smoke is ink on blotting paper.

techniques.name: Scientific register
techniques.definition: Borrowing the vocabulary and cadence of a report or a lecture.
techniques.inThisBook: Distances, volumes, spectrum analysis and anatomical description give the terror a tone of measurement, and the epilogue's admissions of ignorance are more convincing than certainty would be.

quotations.text: No one would have believed in the last years of the nineteenth century that this world was being watched keenly and closely by intelligences greater than man’s and yet as mortal as his own; that as men busied themselves about their various concerns they were scrutinised and studied, perhaps almost as narrowly as a man with a microscope might scrutinise the transient creatures that swarm and multiply in a drop of water.
quotations.analysis: The sentence is built so that the reader is inside the microscope before they know there is one: men are the subject of the verbs for half its length and the object of them by the end. Wells also dates his own book from the future, which guarantees that somebody survived to write it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter I

quotations.text: Yet across the gulf of space, minds that are to our minds as ours are to those of the beasts that perish, intellects vast and cool and unsympathetic, regarded this Earth with envious eyes, and slowly and surely drew their plans against us.
quotations.context: Still in the opening pages, after a paragraph about missionary enterprise.
quotations.analysis: Three adjectives do the work of a whole description of the enemy, and none of them is a moral term: cool and unsympathetic are what a scientist aspires to be. The phrase that follows, drew their plans against us, is the language of a committee, and that is the point.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter I

quotations.text: Are we such apostles of mercy as to complain if the Martians warred in the same spirit?
quotations.context: Immediately after a sentence naming the extermination of the Tasmanians by European settlers.
quotations.analysis: The argument of the whole novel is made in a rhetorical question before the first cylinder has landed. It disarms the reader in advance: any outrage felt over the next two hundred pages has already been booked against an account the reader is on the wrong side of.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter I

quotations.text: The chances against anything manlike on Mars are a million to one
quotations.speaker: Ogilvy
quotations.context: The astronomer, walking home from the observatory, dismissing the idea that the flashes are signals.
quotations.analysis: The professional is not being stupid; he is being reasonable with the evidence he has, which is what makes the line frightening, not comic. Wells gives expertise one confident sentence and then kills the man who says it four chapters later.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter I

quotations.text: A big greyish rounded bulk, the size, perhaps, of a bear, was rising slowly and painfully out of the cylinder. As it bulged up and caught the light, it glistened like wet leather.
quotations.context: The lid of the cylinder falls off and the first Martian appears above the edge of the pit.
quotations.analysis: The first alien in English fiction to be described this closely is measured against a bear and a piece of wet leather, both things a Woking crowd would have handled. Wells withholds the eyes for another sentence, so the thing is an object before it is a gaze.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter IV

quotations.text: It was sweeping round swiftly and steadily, this flaming death, this invisible, inevitable sword of heat.
quotations.context: The deputation with the white flag has just been burned, and the beam is turning towards the narrator.
quotations.analysis: The weapon is named with a word from an older war, sword, because nothing in the narrator's vocabulary fits it. Every adjective is about motion and none about appearance, which is accurate: he is describing something he cannot see, only infer from what catches fire.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter V

quotations.text: A monstrous tripod, higher than many houses, striding over the young pine trees, and smashing them aside in its career; a walking engine of glittering metal, striding now across the heather; articulate ropes of steel dangling from it, and the clattering tumult of its passage mingling with the riot of the thunder.
quotations.context: In a thunderstorm on the Maybury road, with his wife already safe at Leatherhead.
quotations.analysis: The machine is assembled in front of the reader out of participles, each clause adding one moving part, because the narrator is seeing it in lightning flashes, not continuously. A page later he reaches for a milking stool to explain it, and the drop in register is the most honest thing in the chapter.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter X

quotations.text: This must be the beginning of the end
quotations.speaker: The curate
quotations.context: His first extended speech, among the ruins at Weybridge.
quotations.analysis: He has a framework ready and reaches for it immediately, which spares him the work of looking. The novel sets his apocalypse against the narrator's habit of counting cylinders and noting times, and only one of the two men is capable of learning anything new.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter XIII

quotations.text: All the work⁠—all the Sunday schools⁠—What have we done⁠—what has Weybridge done? Everything gone⁠—everything destroyed. The church! We rebuilt it only three years ago. Gone! Swept out of existence! Why?
quotations.speaker: The curate
quotations.context: Standing in the wreckage of his parish.
quotations.analysis: The grief is real and the accounting is parochial: Sunday schools, a church rebuilt three years ago, a single town. He asks why five times in the chapter and never once asks what, which is the difference between him and the man listening to him.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter XIII

quotations.text: It was the beginning of the rout of civilisation, of the massacre of mankind.
quotations.context: Summarising the flight of London, seen as if from a balloon above the home counties.
quotations.analysis: Rout is a military word applied to a population that was never an army, and the sentence puts civilisation and mankind in the same grammatical position as a broken regiment. Wells reaches this judgement only after six pages of specific roads and named suburbs, so the abstraction has been earned.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book I, Chapter XVII

quotations.text: I was no longer a master, but an animal among the animals, under the Martian heel. With us it would be as with them, to lurk and watch, to run and hide; the fear and empire of man had passed away.
quotations.context: Walking through the red weed towards Putney, after seeing navvies digging foundations for a house.
quotations.analysis: The realisation is triggered by the most ordinary sight in the book, men building a house, and the tenses give it away: it would be as with them, the future of a man who has already accepted the position. Empire is the exact word, and it is the same empire the first chapter warned about.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VI

quotations.text: It never was a war, any more than there’s war between man and ants.
quotations.speaker: The artilleryman
quotations.context: On Putney Hill, over the first evening of talk.
quotations.analysis: War implies two parties with something to settle, and the artilleryman is right that this is not one. What he cannot see is that the same argument applies backwards: the analogy he has just used is the one the first chapter used about Europeans and the people they cleared.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VII

quotations.speaker: The artilleryman
quotations.context: Closing his comparison of men with insects.
quotations.analysis: Three words, and the adjective is the horror: ants are cleared out of the way, but these ones are also food. It is the only moment in the novel where the human position is stated as a biological fact, not a political one.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: Cities, nations, civilisation, progress⁠—it’s all over. That game’s up. We’re beat.
quotations.speaker: The artilleryman
quotations.context: Setting out the principle on which he says he has acted.
quotations.analysis: Everything the nineteenth century believed in is listed and dismissed in a sporting idiom. The energy of the speech is what persuades the narrator for a night, and Wells then shows the same man unable to finish a trench, so that the rhetoric and the labour can be compared directly.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VII

quotations.text: And scattered about it, some in their overturned war-machines, some in the now rigid handling-machines, and a dozen of them stark and silent and laid in a row, were the Martians⁠—dead!⁠—slain by the putrefactive and disease bacteria against which their systems were unprepared; slain as the red weed was being slain; slain, after all man’s devices had failed, by the humblest things that God, in his wisdom, has put upon this Earth.
quotations.context: On the rampart of the Martian redoubt on Primrose Hill.
quotations.analysis: Slain is repeated three times, each with a different agent, and the last is the smallest thing in the book. The sentence gives the victory to bacteria and the credit to God, which leaves human courage, artillery and strategy with nothing to claim at all.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VIII

quotations.text: By the toll of a billion deaths man has bought his birthright of the Earth, and it is his against all comers; it would still be his were the Martians ten times as mighty as they are. For neither do men live nor die in vain.
quotations.context: Explaining why the invaders died and human beings did not.
quotations.analysis: Birthright is a legal and biblical word, and Wells insists it was bought, not granted, at a price counted in the deaths of people nobody recorded. It is the closest the novel comes to consolation, and it is addressed to the species, not to anyone in it.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter VIII

quotations.text: We have learned now that we cannot regard this planet as being fenced in and a secure abiding place for Man; we can never anticipate the unseen good or evil that may come upon us suddenly out of space.
quotations.context: The Epilogue, weighing what the invasion has permanently changed.
quotations.analysis: The image is agricultural, a fenced field, and it is the exact opposite of the imperial map: the planet is no longer property. Wells then sidesteps the obvious moral by suggesting the invasion may have done humanity good, which is a colder thought than the one it replaces.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter X

quotations.text: I go to London and see the busy multitudes in Fleet Street and the Strand, and it comes across my mind that they are but the ghosts of the past, haunting the streets that I have seen silent and wretched, going to and fro, phantasms in a dead city, the mockery of life in a galvanised body.
quotations.context: The Epilogue, describing what the narrator still sees years afterwards.
quotations.analysis: The tenses have gone to the present: this is something that goes on happening, more than a memory. The living crowd is described as the ghost and the emptied street as the real one, which inverts the usual arrangement of a haunting.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter X

quotations.text: And strangest of all is it to hold my wife’s hand again, and to think that I have counted her, and that she has counted me, among the dead.
quotations.context: The last sentence of the book.
quotations.analysis: Strangest is a superlative reached after tripods, dead London and the redoubt, and it is spent on two people holding hands. The symmetry of the clause, he counted her and she counted him, makes the loss mutual, and the novel ends on an arithmetic of the dead, not on relief.
quotations.source: Standard Ebooks text, Book II, Chapter X

timeline.label: H. G. Wells born at Bromley
timeline.detail: He later trained in science in South Kensington under T. H. Huxley.

timeline.label: Schiaparelli maps the canali of Mars
timeline.detail: The Italian word for channels was widely read in English as canals, and the idea of Martian engineering entered popular astronomy.

timeline.label: Percival Lowell opens his observatory at Flagstaff
timeline.detail: Built largely to study Mars; the novel opens with a light seen on the planet at the 1894 opposition.

timeline.label: The Time Machine published
timeline.detail: Wells's first scientific romance, and the beginning of four years that also produced Moreau, The Invisible Man and this book.

timeline.label: The Island of Doctor Moreau published
timeline.detail: Its interest in the boundary between men and animals runs straight into the artilleryman's argument about ants.

timeline.label: Serialised in Pearson's Magazine
timeline.detail: British readers met the invasion in monthly instalments; an American serial ran in Cosmopolitan.

timeline.label: First book edition, William Heinemann
timeline.detail: Harper and Brothers issued the American book edition the same year.

timeline.label: Orson Welles broadcasts the story on CBS
timeline.detail: Howard Koch's adaptation moved the first landing to Grovers Mill, New Jersey, and used the form of a news bulletin.

timeline.label: Wells dies in London
timeline.detail: By then he was known as much for his histories and political writing as for the scientific romances.

timeline.label: George Pal's film released
timeline.detail: Directed by Byron Haskin, it relocated the invasion to mid-century America and replaced the tripods with flying machines.

timeline.label: Jeff Wayne's musical version released
timeline.detail: A concept album narrated by Richard Burton, which kept the novel's structure of a witness reporting after the event.

timeline.label: Steven Spielberg's film released
timeline.detail: Refocused on one family in flight, and on the refugee traffic that occupies the brother's chapters.

places.name: Horsell Common, Woking
places.note: Where the first cylinder falls, into a sandpit on ordinary common land.

places.name: Ottershaw
places.note: Ogilvy's observatory, where the narrator watches the flashes on Mars.

places.name: Leatherhead
places.note: Where the narrator leaves his wife with cousins, and where he is taken in at the end.

places.name: Shepperton
places.note: Where artillery brings down a fighting-machine and the Thames is boiled by the wreck.

places.name: Putney Hill
places.note: The house where the artilleryman explains the underground future of the human race.

places.name: Primrose Hill
places.note: The Martian redoubt over dead London, where the invaders are found killed by bacteria.

criticalViews.summary: The reading the book invites in its own first chapter: Britain is made to suffer what British settlers did to peoples they judged inferior, and the novel's sympathies are complicated by the narrator's inability to claim any moral advantage.
criticalViews.counter: The Martians are still presented as biologically alien, not as colonists with a culture, which lets the comparison work as shock without holding up in detail.

criticalViews.position: A founding text of science fiction
criticalViews.summary: Wells's method, extrapolating from published science and grounding the result in real streets and timetables, set the pattern for the invasion narrative and for a century of catastrophe fiction.
criticalViews.counter: Read only as an origin, the book's peculiar features go missing: its dead time, its long passages of hunger and boredom, and its refusal to give anyone a decisive action.

criticalViews.summary: Critics have placed the novel beside invasion-scare fiction, anxieties about national decline and the popular astronomy of the 1890s, reading it as a diagnosis of a society that has mistaken technical superiority for permanence.
criticalViews.counter: The epilogue argues the opposite way, suggesting that losing serene confidence in the future was worth what it cost.

essayQuestions.question: How far does The War of the Worlds ask its readers to see themselves as the Martians?
essayQuestions.focus: Imperial reversal and the novel's first chapter
plan: Start with the Tasmanians sentence in Book I, Chapter I: the comparison is made before any Martian acts.
Trace the vocabulary of empire through the book, especially the narrator's realisation that he is under the Martian heel.
Use the exodus chapters to show English people occupying the position of a displaced population.
Test the limits of the case: the Martians take blood, not land, and never speak or govern.
Close on the ending, where deliverance is microbial, so no imperial self-justification is available.

essayQuestions.question: What is gained by telling the invasion through a narrator who achieves nothing?
essayQuestions.focus: Narration, authority and the second witness
plan: Establish what the narrator actually does: walks, hides, watches, and writes it up years later.
Contrast him with the artilleryman, who has a plan, and the curate, who has an explanation.
Examine the brother's chapters as a deliberate widening, and ask how the narrator could know them.
Consider the epilogue’s admissions of ignorance as a source of credibility, not a weakness.
Judge whether the book's power depends on this refusal of a hero, comparing any adaptation that supplies one.

essayQuestions.question: Discuss Wells's use of real places and ordinary objects in the novel.
essayQuestions.focus: Topography, simile and the texture of catastrophe
plan: Map the route: Horsell, Byfleet, Weybridge, Sheen, Putney, Primrose Hill, and what naming them does to a local reader.
Collect the domestic comparisons, from the milking stool to ink on blotting paper, and note who is making them.
Show how the Black Smoke and the red weed are described in the language of gardening and public health.
Set the scientific register of the epilogue against the eyewitness register of the middle books.
Conclude on the effect: terror produced by accuracy, not invention.

essayQuestions.question: 'The ending is a defeat for humanity, not a victory.' Discuss.
plan: Set out how the Martians die and how little any human action contributes to it.
Read the humblest things sentence closely, noting the three uses of slain and where the agency lies.
Weigh the billion deaths passage, which does claim something for the species, though nothing for individuals.
Use the epilogue's fenced-in image and the return of the narrator's nightmares against any sense of restoration.
Decide what the last sentence about his wife's hand settles, and what it deliberately leaves open.

discussionQuestions: The first chapter tells you the Martians are only doing what Europeans have already done. Does knowing that change how you read the rest of the invasion?
The artilleryman talks brilliantly and digs almost nothing. Why does Wells let him be so persuasive first?
The narrator kills the curate. Does the novel condemn him for it?
Nothing the army does makes any difference, and the Thunder Child dies achieving one small thing. Why keep the episode at all?
Would the book be more or less frightening if the Martians could speak?

related.why: The same decade's other story of an invader arriving by sea, tracked through timetables, telegrams and newspaper cuttings.
Wilde’s novel of the 1890s, taking the other route out of Victorian confidence: inward, not outward.
The earlier argument about what science makes and what it fails to anticipate.
A contemporary English fantasy that also sets one isolated narrator against forces with no interest in him.
Another late-Victorian scientific romance told through documents by a narrator who arrives after the event.
